content: A trauma center is a specialized hospital designed to function as a critical care facility for emergency medical services, providing the highest level of care for patients with traumatic injuries 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. These centers were established in recognition of the fact that traumatic injuries often require immediate and complex surgical interventions to save lives. To qualify as a trauma center, a hospital must meet specific criteria, including the presence of a high-quality intensive care unit and an operating room that is fully staffed and operational around the clock. Trauma services are led by a team of trauma surgeons, often supported by specialists such as neurosurgeons and orthopedic surgeons. Many trauma centers are equipped with a helipad to facilitate the rapid transport of patients via medical evacuation (MEDEVAC). The operation of a trauma center is highly resource-intensive and expensive. Due to these costs, some regions are underserved by trauma centers. For example, Harborview Medical Center in Seattle, Washington, serves not only the state of Washington but also Idaho, Montana, and Alaska. Similarly, the Orlando Regional Medical Center in Florida, originally built to serve five counties, now provides care for patients from more than twenty counties. Despite these challenges, patients injured in remote areas and transported to a trauma center by helicopter often receive faster and more effective care than those injured in urban areas and taken to a standard hospital by ground ambulance. In the United States, trauma centers are categorized into levels based on the resources they provide and the volume of patients they treat annually. Level I centers offer the most comprehensive services, while lower levels provide more limited care. Some trauma centers specialize in either adult or pediatric care. The concept of the trauma center originated at the University of Maryland, Baltimore, during the 1960s and 1970s, spearheaded by heart surgeon and shock researcher Dr. R. Adams Cowley. He founded the Shock Trauma Center in Baltimore in 1961. Cook County Hospital in Chicago, Illinois, claims to have opened the first trauma center in the United States in 1966. Dr. David R. Boyd, who interned at Cook County Hospital from 1963 to 1964 before serving in the U.S. Army, became the first shock-trauma fellow at the Shock Trauma Center from 1967 to 1968. He later returned to Cook County Hospital, where he served as the resident director of the Cook County Trauma Unit. Trauma centers are classified into four levels, which reflect the types of resources available and the number of patients treated annually. These levels are based on national standards for trauma care in hospitals, as developed and recommended by the American College of Surgeons.
